items.title: OPEC+ supply policy and spare capacity
items.mechanism: OPEC+ sets production targets for its members, and OPEC members hold almost all of the world's spare production capacity. A change in targets can move crude prices when it changes the market's view of future supply, but what matters in the end is the output actually delivered, and members do not always produce at their targets. Spare capacity is a buffer: when it is ample, lost supply elsewhere can be replaced; when it is thin, crude tends to carry a larger risk premium. Producers outside the group tend to run near capacity and respond to price, which can erode the effect of a cut over time.
direction: Cuts to targets that are delivered as announced tend to support crude prices, other things equal; increases tend to weigh on them.
Output above targets, or doubts about compliance, tends to weaken the support that announced cuts provide.
Thin spare capacity tends to make crude more sensitive to any disruption; ample spare capacity tends to damp that sensitivity.
The effect tends to fall first on crude. Product prices tend to move with crude, so the 3-2-1 crack need not change much, unless the change alters the mix of crude grades refiners can buy.
changes_when: Members produce well above their targets, or the group's cohesion weakens, so announcements carry less weight.
Demand is weakening at the same time, so a cut may slow a fall in prices rather than lift them.
Supply from producers outside the group responds to the price and grows, which can offset a cut over time.
A decision is already anticipated by the market, so the announcement itself moves prices little.
The group shifts from defending prices to defending market share and adds barrels even into a weak market.

items.title: Global demand: growth, industry and the fuel mix
items.mechanism: Oil demand tends to rise with economic activity. In emerging economies such as China and India, where industry and transport are growing, growth tends to add more oil use than in the United States and Europe, where services weigh more and efficiency rules slow consumption. Demand is not one number: diesel tends to follow freight, manufacturing and farming; gasoline follows driving, income and employment; jet fuel follows air travel. Broad growth tends to lift crude. A shift in which fuel is wanted can move one product's price, and so the crack, more than crude.
direction: Stronger global growth tends to lift oil demand and crude prices; a slowdown tends to weigh on them.
Strong freight and industrial activity tends to support diesel prices and the diesel part of the crack.
Strong driving demand tends to support gasoline prices and the gasoline part of the crack.
Rising air travel tends to support jet fuel, which draws on the same middle-distillate part of the barrel as diesel, and so can tighten diesel too.
A better growth outlook can lift futures prices and encourage holding stocks, which can raise prompt prices as well.
changes_when: Supply adjusts at the same time, so stronger demand is met by more output or by stock draws rather than by a rise in price.
Efficiency standards, electric vehicles or biofuels reduce the fuel needed for a given level of activity.
Growth is concentrated in services rather than manufacturing and freight, which use less oil per unit of output.
Demand responds to price as well as to income: when fuel becomes dearer, households and firms use less of it, a little in the short run and more over years.
Apparent demand reflects restocking rather than end use, so it fades once stocks are rebuilt.

items.title: Inventories: crude stocks and product stocks
items.mechanism: Inventories balance supply and demand and cushion shocks. Crude and product stocks tell different stories: crude stocks reflect the balance between producers and refiners, product stocks that between refiners and end users. When stocks are low, prices tend to react more to a disruption. Low gasoline or distillate stocks tend to lift product prices relative to crude, widening the crack; low crude stocks tend to lift crude itself. Stocks and the futures curve move together: stocks tend to build when later prices cover storage costs, and prompt barrels tend to gain a premium when stocks run low.
direction: Crude draws larger than usual for the season tend to support crude prices; builds larger than usual tend to weigh on them.
Gasoline or distillate stocks that are low for the time of year tend to support product prices and widen the crack.
Product stocks that are high for the time of year tend to compress the crack, even when crude is firm.
Near-dated futures priced above later ones tend to go with stock draws; the reverse tends to go with stock builds.
changes_when: Stock changes reflect timing, such as delayed import cargoes or a swing in exports, rather than a change in the underlying balance.
A level is read without its season: product stocks normally fall in some months and rise in others.
Barrels move to places outside the headline figure, such as other regions or storage at sea.
Governments release emergency stocks or refill them, adding or removing barrels outside the commercial market.
A single weekly figure is noisy and later revised, so one week can mislead.
A draw or build the market had anticipated tends to move prices less than one that surprises it.

items.title: Refining capacity, utilization and outages
items.mechanism: This is the main channel for the crack, the gap between product prices and crude. Anything that changes how much refined product reaches a market, without changing crude by as much, acts mainly on it. Planned maintenance and unplanned outages, such as fires or hurricanes, cut product supply; whether they widen the crack depends on stocks and on how quickly other supply can arrive. Closures can tighten a region's product balance over time, and new capacity elsewhere can loosen it. Refiners can shift output between gasoline and distillates only within limits, so product cracks can diverge.
direction: An outage tends to widen the crack in the affected region when stocks are already low and alternative supply is not readily available.
When utilization is high there is little room to raise output, so extra demand tends to show up in wider cracks rather than more product.
Closures tend to support a region's product prices relative to crude and to raise its reliance on imported product.
New capacity, especially export-oriented plants abroad, tends to weigh on cracks in the markets those plants supply.
Because yields are only partly flexible, a shortage of one product can lift its crack while another product's crack stays weak.
A large outage also cuts the refinery's crude purchases, which can soften local crude prices while product prices firm.
Low margins can lead refiners to cut runs, which trims product supply and can pull cracks back toward refiners' running costs.
changes_when: Product stocks are ample, so an outage passes with little price effect.
The link can be weak on average: outages large enough to move monthly prices have been uncommon.
Imports can arrive quickly, which limits how far a regional crack can rise above the cost of bringing product in.
Product demand is weak at the same time, so lower output meets lower use.
Repairs finish or supply chains adjust; the price effects of outages have tended to be short-lived.

items.title: Geopolitics: conflict, sanctions and the risk premium
items.mechanism: Wars, sanctions and attacks on export infrastructure can remove barrels or threaten to. Prices can move before any barrel is lost: when disruption is feared and spare capacity or stocks look thin, prices can sit above what current supply and demand alone would support, a risk premium. Sanctions often reroute trade rather than remove it, lengthening voyages and raising costs. A measure that hits refined products, such as diesel, acts more on product prices and the crack; one that hits crude acts more on crude. Effects have tended to fade as trade adjusts to new routes.
direction: A credible threat to a major producer or route tends to add a risk premium to crude, even before supply changes.
Measures that cut a large product exporter out of a market tend to raise product prices and cracks in the importing region, as buyers turn to more distant suppliers.
Supply disruptions tend to steepen backwardation, as prompt barrels become more valuable than later ones.
The easing of a threat, or sanctions that prove porous, tend to remove the premium.
changes_when: Spare capacity or emergency stocks are ample, so lost barrels can be replaced.
Sanctioned barrels keep flowing through other buyers and routes, so global supply changes less than the measure suggests.
The event is already priced in, so its occurrence moves prices little or even lowers them.

During a conflict that constrains supply, futures prices can sit above where investors think spot prices are heading, as buyers pay to hedge against further rises, so the curve overstates the prices investors anticipate.
Weak demand offsets the supply risk.

items.title: Shipping: chokepoints, freight and insurance
items.mechanism: Most traded oil moves by sea, much of it through a few narrow passages. A blockage or threat at a chokepoint can delay supply and raise freight and war-risk insurance costs, and rerouting onto longer voyages ties up ships, which can lift freight on other lanes too. Freight separates regional prices: a price gap between two markets must cover the cost of shipping before cargoes move. When freight rises, regional prices can drift apart and product arbitrage between regions can close, which can firm cracks in importing regions and soften them in exporting ones.
direction: Higher freight and insurance costs tend to raise delivered prices in importing regions and lower what exporters receive.
When freight is expensive, a wider regional price gap is needed before trade flows; cheap freight tends to narrow regional spreads.
Regions that import products tend to see firmer product prices and cracks when product tanker rates rise; exporting regions may see the reverse.
A disruption at a major crude chokepoint tends to act on crude first; one on a product route acts more on product prices.
changes_when: Pipelines or other routes can bypass the chokepoint, though often for only part of the volume.
The tanker fleet has spare capacity, so rerouting lifts freight only a little.
Stocks near consuming regions cover the delay while cargoes take longer routes.
Exporters with few other outlets absorb the higher freight, so importers pay little more.

items.title: The dollar, interest rates and growth expectations
items.mechanism: Oil is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar can make it cheaper for buyers outside the United States, supporting demand and prices; a stronger dollar can do the reverse. The link is not stable: the dollar and oil have often moved in opposite directions but can move together, as when the United States is a net energy exporter and dearer oil raises its export earnings. Higher real interest rates raise the cost of holding stocks and tend to slow activity, which can weigh on crude, more through activity than storage. Growth outlooks and risk appetite can move oil alongside equities.
direction: A broad dollar depreciation can support crude prices through demand from buyers outside the United States; an appreciation can weigh on them.
A rise in real interest rates can lower crude prices at short horizons, mainly by slowing activity rather than by raising the cost of holding stocks; the effect tends to be modest.
An improving growth outlook tends to lift crude together with equities; a deteriorating one tends to weigh on both.
Strong investor inflows into oil futures can add to price moves, but flows can follow prices as well as lead them, so heavy buying need not mean that the flows set prices.
changes_when: The dollar and oil respond to a common shock, such as news about US growth, so they move together rather than apart.
Oil shocks can themselves move the dollar, so a correlation alone does not show which way an effect runs.
A supply shock dominates, raising oil while hurting growth, so oil can move against equities rather than with them.
Beyond the first quarter or so, the sign and size of interest-rate effects on oil are uncertain.

items.title: Seasonality in the Northern Hemisphere
items.mechanism: Fuel demand and refinery maintenance follow the seasons, so product prices and the crack tend to move in a yearly pattern. These patterns are for the Northern Hemisphere, where most refining and fuel demand sit. Gasoline demand tends to rise into the summer driving season, and summer-grade gasoline costs more to make, so its price tends to rise through spring. Distillate use tends to rise in autumn and winter with heating and harvests, so its stocks are usually built in summer. Planned maintenance tends to cluster in late winter, early spring and autumn, when product demand is lowest.
direction: Gasoline prices and the gasoline part of the crack tend to strengthen in spring, ahead of the summer driving season, and to ease after it.
Distillate prices and the diesel part of the crack tend to find support in autumn and winter, when heating and harvest demand add to freight use.
A heavy maintenance season tends to lower refinery output and product stocks, which can firm cracks while refiners buy less crude.
Gasoline stocks tend to fall through the summer driving season, and distillate stocks tend to peak in summer, when distillate use is lowest.
changes_when: Weather departs from normal: a mild winter can weaken distillate demand, and a severe cold spell can strain heating oil supply.
A hurricane or an unplanned outage during the season outweighs the usual pattern.
Stocks enter a season well above or below their usual range, which can mute or amplify the seasonal move.
Maintenance is lighter or heavier than usual, or moves earlier or later.
Regional fuel rules differ, so the timing of the grade change and its price effect varies by region.

items.trigger: Jet fuel price: a middle distillate, so crude plus the distillate crack
items.effect_text: Airline margins tend to narrow when jet fuel costs rise faster than fares can follow. Fuel is one of the largest airline costs. Jet fuel is a middle distillate, priced alongside diesel, so it can become dearer through a wider distillate crack even when crude is steady, and carriers that manage fuel risk mainly through crude stay exposed to that crack. The size, and even the sign, depends on why fuel moved: if it rises with strong travel demand, carriers can often lift fares; if a supply shock raises it while demand is weak, the squeeze tends to be sharper.
second_order: Carriers can trim capacity on weaker routes, which can lift fares and seat occupancy on the routes that remain.
Air fares are part of consumer prices, so a jet fuel shock can reach measured inflation through transport services.
Tourism, air cargo, airports and aircraft makers can feel slower traffic growth if fares stay high for long.
flips_when: Hedges lock in earlier fuel prices for a time, which delays or cushions the effect; hedging practice differs widely across airlines and regions.
Fuel rises with strong global growth while capacity is tight, so carriers can pass fuel costs on to fares and margins can hold up.
The distillate crack narrows while crude rises, so jet fuel rises by less than crude.
The dollar moves: fuel is priced in dollars, so a carrier earning other currencies gains when the dollar weakens and loses when it strengthens.
Fuel changes gradually rather than in a sudden jump, which gives carriers time to adjust fares and schedules.
items.lag: Large fuel moves can hit margins in the short term, and costs tend to pass through to fares as and when capacity can adjust; hedges can delay the effect for some carriers.

items.trigger: Bunker fuel for ships and diesel for trucks: product prices, not crude
items.effect_text: Carriers that index fuel surcharges to published fuel prices can pass much of a fuel rise on to shippers, so the cost tends to fall on cargo owners; carriers on fixed rates, or facing spare ships and trucks, absorb more of it. Bunker fuel is its own set of products, from heavy fuel oil to low-sulfur fuel oil and marine gasoil, priced partly by sulfur content, so it need not move one for one with crude. Diesel is a middle distillate and can move with the distillate crack as well as crude. Freight rates also depend on demand and fleet capacity, often more than on fuel.
second_order: Freight costs feed into import and producer prices and can reach consumer goods prices, more so where imports are a large share of consumption.
Retailers and manufacturers can absorb part of the cost for a while, which delays and dilutes its pass-through to shelf prices.
Shippers can switch routes or modes, for example from road to rail, when fuel changes relative transport costs.
flips_when: Freight demand is weak and capacity ample, so carriers compete and absorb fuel costs rather than pass them on.
Contracts fix rates without a fuel clause, which leaves the cost with the carrier until renewal.
The premium of low-sulfur over high-sulfur marine fuel moves, which changes the cost advantage of scrubber-fitted ships.
Freight demand surges or ships are scarce, so rates move far more than fuel costs alone would imply.
Ships slow down to save fuel, which cuts fuel use per voyage but ties up more vessels and can tighten capacity.
items.lag: Fuel surcharges indexed to published diesel prices can adjust as those prices are updated; freight costs tend to reach import and producer prices within months, and consumer prices more slowly, over many months.

items.trigger: The crack (product prices less crude) and the crude price itself
chain: The crack: a benchmark gross margin
items.effect_text: Upstream producers tend to gain from a rise in crude, while refiners gain when the crack widens and lose when crude rises faster than products. Strong product demand, or refinery outages elsewhere, can widen the crack even with crude flat; a supply-led rise in crude that products do not match narrows it. The crack is a benchmark for the gross margin; a refiner's own margin also depends on the crude it buys and the products it yields, and the crack leaves out energy, labour, maintenance and compliance costs. Integrated companies are partly offset across the two businesses.
second_order: Sustained wide cracks can lift refinery runs and product supply; narrow cracks can lead refiners to cut runs and weaker plants to close.
Stronger upstream cash flow can fund more drilling, which can add crude supply after a delay.
Oil-exporting economies and their governments gain revenue while importing economies lose income: a shift in the terms of trade.
flips_when: Crude rises on a supply cut while product demand is soft, so products lag and refiners' margins narrow.
Products firm on refinery outages or strong demand, so the crack widens even if crude is flat.
The refiner's crude trades at a widening discount to the benchmark crude, so its margin can hold up even when the benchmark crack narrows.
Producers have hedged future output, so for a time they gain less from a crude rise and lose less from a fall.
Refinery fuel and hydrogen costs, often tied to natural gas, climb and erode net margins even when the gross crack is wide.
Costs for drilling services rise with activity, or the tax take increases, so less of a crude rise reaches producers.
items.lag: The crack moves with daily product and crude prices, while reported margins can lag through crude purchase timing and inventory accounting; new supply tends to follow after months for shale and years for conventional projects.

items.trigger: Naphtha (priced off crude) against ethane (anchored by natural gas)
items.effect_text: Producers using gas-based ethane can gain when oil rises relative to gas, while those using oil-based naphtha can face a cost squeeze when product prices do not keep up. Naphtha is the main cracker feedstock in Europe and much of Asia; ethane, whose price has natural gas as its floor, is the main one in the United States and much of the Middle East. If naphtha-based plants set the marginal cost of ethylene, product prices can follow oil while ethane costs do not. Naphtha crackers also yield valuable coproducts, such as propylene, which offset part of the squeeze.
second_order: Plastics and packaging costs can pass to makers of consumer goods, though slowly and only in part.
Regions with cheap ethane can gain export share in ethylene derivatives, while naphtha-based plants elsewhere run less.
Weak margins can lead naphtha-based producers to cut runs or close older plants.
flips_when: Natural gas rises relative to oil, which narrows or reverses the ethane advantage.
Cracker or export demand for ethane is tight, so its price can pull away from gas toward propane and the advantage narrows.
Plastics demand is weak, so neither route can pass feedstock costs on and margins narrow for both.
Coproduct values are high, which supports naphtha crackers' returns.
Crackers that can switch feedstocks move toward the cheaper one, which narrows the gap.
items.lag: Feedstock costs can reach ethylene and polymer prices within weeks to months, often through monthly contract prices; the effect on finished goods tends to be slower and partial.

items.trigger: Farm diesel, and natural gas (not Brent) for nitrogen fertilizer
items.effect_text: Farm margins tend to narrow when diesel and fertilizer costs rise faster than crop prices. Nitrogen fertilizer follows natural gas, not Brent: gas is the main input to ammonia, the base of nitrogen fertilizers, so an oil move reaches fertilizer only insofar as gas moves with it. Diesel, a product price, is the main fuel used directly on farms. Exposure differs by crop: corn and rice carry higher energy-related costs per acre than soybeans. Dearer energy can reduce output and lift crop prices, which offsets part of the squeeze.
second_order: Energy costs can add to food prices, though more through processing, transport and retail than through farm inputs.
Livestock producers can face dearer feed when energy lifts crop costs.
Nitrogen producers in regions with cheap gas can gain, since fertilizer prices tend to be set by the marginal, higher-cost producer.
Where fertilizer is costly, farmers can apply less or shift acreage toward less nitrogen-intensive crops such as soybeans.
flips_when: Grain markets are strong at the same time, so crop revenue offsets the cost.
Crops that feed biofuels, such as corn for ethanol, can firm with oil, which can offset or outweigh the cost rise for growers.
Natural gas stays cheap while oil rises, so fertilizer costs hold steady and only diesel bites.
Farmers bought fertilizer or fuel ahead, which delays the effect until the next purchase.
Fertilizer made where gas is cheap can be imported, which caps costs in regions where gas is dear, subject to shipping costs.
Over time farmers adjust crops and practices, so the longer-run effect tends to be smaller than the initial one.
items.lag: The squeeze on farm income tends to be largest in the short run and to shrink as farmers adjust crops and practices.

items.trigger: Pump prices of gasoline and diesel: retail prices, not crude
items.effect_text: Dearer fuel tends to weaken discretionary spending. Gasoline demand responds little in the short run, so a rise at the pump mainly leaves households less to spend on other things, like a tax on real income; when fuel gets cheaper, households tend to spend the saving on other things rather than hold it. Lower-income households, for whom fuel takes a larger share of income, tend to feel it most. For fuel retailers the effect is mixed: pump prices adjust with a delay, so their margins tend to narrow while wholesale costs climb and widen when those costs fall.
second_order: Weaker spending at restaurants, on travel and in other discretionary outlets can slow growth in consumer-facing sectors.
Households can drive less and, over years, choose more efficient vehicles, which trims fuel demand.
Spending can shift toward essentials and cheaper brands, which can favour discount retailers over discretionary ones.
flips_when: Crude moves pass only partly to the pump, since crude is one cost among refining, distribution and taxes.
Wages and employment are strong at the same time, as in a demand-led boom, so real incomes hold up.
Households see the rise as temporary and draw on savings rather than cut other spending.
The economy is a net oil producer, so producer income and investment offset part of the drag.
When fuel gets cheaper, the same channel supports discretionary spending, and fuel retailers' margins tend to widen for a time.
items.lag: Pump prices tend to follow crude within weeks, though not fully or at once, and the spending response tends to build over weeks and months.

items.trigger: Retail fuel prices (energy in the consumer price index), which follow crude
chain: Indirect: energy costs in other prices
Central bank: look through, or tighten
items.effect_text: The direct effect is mechanical: fuels are part of the consumer price index, so headline inflation moves with them. Indirect effects come as energy costs pass into transport and other goods and services; this is how oil can reach core inflation, an effect that tends to be small but can last. Second-round effects are distinct and only possible: they arise if wages and inflation expectations start to respond. A central bank may look through a temporary energy shock when expectations are anchored and wage growth restrained, or tighten if second-round effects appear or inflation is already high.
second_order: Dearer energy also weighs on real incomes and spending in importing economies, which can damp demand and, in time, inflation itself.
Exporters' terms of trade improve and importers' worsen, which can move exchange rates and spread the shock across countries.
Bond yields and the pricing of policy rates can shift as markets judge how the central bank may respond.
flips_when: Inflation expectations are well anchored and wages are not indexed to prices, which makes second-round effects less likely.
Inflation is already above target or the labour market is tight at the start, which raises second-round risk and the case for tightening.
The energy rise is persistent rather than a one-off jump, giving indirect effects longer to build.
A one-off jump in the energy price level leaves the annual inflation rate after a year; a quick reversal unwinds it sooner.
Fuel taxes, subsidies or price caps differ, changing how much of a crude move reaches consumer prices.
A demand-led rise, with strong activity, strengthens the case to tighten; a supply cut that hurts growth poses a trade-off between inflation and growth.
items.lag: The direct effect on headline inflation tends to appear quickly, as pump prices adjust; indirect effects build more slowly and can linger in core inflation for a long time.
